questions.question: Surah Saba opens with 'All praise is due to Allah' and extends that praise beyond the present world. What does verse 1 say about the scope of divine praise in relation to time?
options: A. Praise belongs to Allah only in this world, since the Hereafter is a different realm governed by different rules
B. Praise belongs to Allah in both this world and the Hereafter, affirming that His sovereignty is not limited by time or dimension
C. Praise is shared between Allah and His prophets in this world, and becomes solely Allah's in the Hereafter
D. Praise is owed to Allah only after blessings are received, not as a constant and ongoing acknowledgment
questions.explanation: Verse 1 declares that all praise belongs to Allah in both this life and the Hereafter. As Sayyid Qutb writes in Fi Zilal al-Quran, the dual mention of praise frames history as a single continuous narrative encompassed by divine praise, and the divine names al-Hakim and al-Khabir that close the verse ground this in Allah's perfect wisdom and complete awareness.

questions.question: True or false: Verse 2 of Surah Saba pairs a description of Allah's all-encompassing knowledge with the divine names al-Rahim and al-Ghafur, indicating that His total awareness of every deed is coupled with mercy and forgiveness rather than harsh judgment alone.
questions.explanation: Verse 2 enumerates four categories of cosmic movement that Allah knows completely, then closes with al-Rahim and al-Ghafur. Shaykh Muhammad al-Sha'rawi observed that this pairing is itself an act of divine teaching: knowledge without mercy is terror, but knowledge paired with mercy is guidance — a combination that distinguishes Quranic theology from fatalistic worldviews.

questions.question: In verse 3, the Prophet is commanded to answer the disbelievers' denial of the Hour with a solemn oath. What oath formula does the verse use, and why did classical Sunni scholars consider it especially significant?
options: A. He swears by the Quran — scholars regarded this as the highest oath since the Quran is the word of Allah
B. He swears by his own truthfulness, reminding the Arabs of his title al-Amin earned before prophethood
C. He swears 'by my Lord,' an unusually emphatic formula that scholars say places the full weight of prophethood behind the testimony
D. He swears by the heavens and the earth, mirroring the cosmic oaths of the shorter Meccan surahs
questions.explanation: The formula 'wa rabbi' (by my Lord) is rare and particularly solemn. Ibn Uthaymeen explained that when the Prophet swears by Allah, the entire weight of prophethood stands behind that testimony, and no one who accepts Muhammad's truthfulness can rationally doubt what he so emphatically affirms.

questions.question: True or false: According to Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, and al-Tabari, the 'kitab mubin' (clear register) mentioned in verse 3 is identified by the scholarly consensus as al-Lawh al-Mahfuz — the Preserved Tablet in which all destined events are recorded.
questions.explanation: The classical Sunni scholars are unanimous on this point: Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, and al-Tabari all identify the 'kitab mubin' as al-Lawh al-Mahfuz. Al-Qurtubi draws the theological conclusion that since Allah's knowledge of every deed is recorded with perfect precision, not even the weight of an atom is lost from the account, making His final judgment perfectly just.

questions.question: Verse 10 describes the special bounty Allah granted to Prophet Dawud. Which two miraculous gifts are specifically mentioned in this verse?
options: A. The ability to walk on water and to understand the language of all birds and animals
B. Mountains and birds commanded to echo his glorifications alongside him, and the softening of iron in his hands
C. Dominion over the jinn and a spring of molten copper granted to him personally
D. A kingdom greater than all other rulers and the prophetic gift of healing the sick by touch
questions.explanation: Verse 10 records two specific gifts: Allah commanded the mountains and birds to repeat praises with Dawud, and He softened iron for him. Ibn Kathir notes that Dawud was the first to fashion chainmail in history — iron became workable in his hands without fire or hammer, and he used this gift to craft coats of mail as commanded in verse 11.

questions.question: True or false: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir argues that even though Allah softened iron for Dawud miraculously, the immediate command to 'calculate precisely the links' of the chainmail shows that divine gifts do not exempt the believer from the obligation of skilled, disciplined effort — a principle al-Zuhayli calls 'active gratitude.'
questions.explanation: Al-Zuhayli identifies this as a Quranic model: the miracle came from Allah, yet the command is immediately to work, measure, and perfect. The verse closes with 'Indeed I am Seeing what you do,' linking quality craftsmanship to divine accountability. Sayyid Qutb adds that the plural command 'Work righteousness' extends this obligation beyond Dawud to all who receive gifts from Allah.

questions.question: Verse 12 describes the wind that Allah subjected to Sulayman. What does the verse say about the distances it would cover?
options: A. The wind traveled from one end of the earth to the other in a single journey each day
B. The wind carried Sulayman's throne across seven seas within seven hours
C. The wind's morning journey covered a month's travel distance and its afternoon journey likewise covered a month's distance
D. The wind transported the jinn armies but was limited to traveling one week's distance per day
questions.explanation: Verse 12 specifies that the subjugated wind's morning journey equaled a full month's travel distance, and its afternoon journey likewise equaled a month. Ibn Kathir notes this miracle demonstrates how Allah suspends natural laws for His prophets, granting them dominion over creation as a sign of their divine commission and the completeness of their authority.

questions.question: After describing the remarkable works the jinn produced for Sulayman, verse 13 delivers a direct divine command and closes with a sobering observation. What does Allah command and what does He observe?
options: A. He commands them to pray continuously, and observes that few of His servants are obedient in their worship
B. He commands the family of Dawud to work in gratitude, and observes that few of His servants are truly grateful
C. He commands them to maintain the great buildings, and observes that most of His servants neglect their responsibilities
D. He commands them to give generously to the poor, and observes that charity is rare among the prosperous
questions.explanation: Verse 13 commands 'Work, O family of David, in gratitude,' then closes: 'and few of My servants are grateful.' Muhammad al-Sha'rawi highlighted the contrast between the immense civilizational grandeur just described and this simple demand for gratitude, arguing that the surah intentionally pairs the family of Dawud — who heed this command — with the people of Saba who follow, as an illustration of the two possible responses to divine blessing.

questions.question: True or false: Imam al-Qurtubi and Fakhr al-Din al-Razi both cite the story of Sulayman's death going undetected by the jinn in verse 14 as one of the strongest Quranic proofs that jinn do not possess knowledge of the unseen, since they continued laboring for an extended period unaware that their master had died.
questions.explanation: Al-Qurtubi states the verse is among the strongest Quranic refutations of jinn knowledge of the ghayb: had they possessed any such knowledge, the incident would have been impossible. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi argues philosophically that the strict Quranic position is that al-ghayb al-mutlaq (absolute unseen knowledge) belongs to Allah alone, and Ibn Uthaymeen applied this directly against claims of fortune-tellers who claim to receive hidden knowledge through jinn.

questions.question: Verse 15 introduces the people of Saba and describes the divine sign placed in their homeland. What was the specific nature of the blessing and what command accompanied it?
options: A. A great navigable river; they were told to build fleets and trade widely across the known world
B. Two magnificent gardens on their right and left; they were told to eat from their Lord's provision and be grateful
C. A network of gold and silver mines; they were told to spend in Allah's way and fund the building of temples
D. A valley of fragrant medicinal herbs; they were told to share them freely with neighboring peoples
questions.explanation: Verse 15 describes two gardens flanking the Sabaean civilization alongside the divine command: 'Eat from the provisions of your Lord and be grateful to Him.' Al-Tabari cites scholarly consensus identifying these as the agricultural abundance sustained by the Ma'rib dam. Ibn Kathir records narrations that the land was so blessed it was reportedly free of harmful insects, snakes, and scorpions — described as an earthly paradise.

questions.question: True or false: According to Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir, the destruction of Saba's civilization by the dam-burst flood described in verse 16 was not only a divine punishment but also a natural consequence of their having abandoned the spiritual and ethical framework that had enabled them to steward their resources wisely.
questions.explanation: Al-Zuhayli notes that the Sabaeans' ingratitude eroded the spiritual foundation that had sustained their wise stewardship, making the dam-burst both divine judgment and natural consequence. He points to the archaeological evidence at Marib in Yemen confirming the historical collapse, and argues this civilizational template warns modern Muslim communities who enjoy prosperity but have become detached from Islamic values.

questions.question: Verse 17 ends the Saba narrative with the rhetorical question: 'Do We repay except the ungrateful?' How did Imam al-Tabari characterize the grammatical and rhetorical force of this question?
options: A. He called it a general threat applying to every believer who falls short in any act of worship

B. He identified it as an istifham inkari — a rhetorical question whose force affirms that this total, comprehensive form of worldly punishment is reserved specifically for extreme, persistent ingratitude, not ordinary human failings
C. He explained it as a legal ruling establishing collective punishment whenever any member of a community commits even a minor sin
D. He read it as reassurance that Allah punishes nobody at all in this world, deferring all recompense to the Hereafter
questions.explanation: Al-Tabari explains the question as istifham inkari — a rhetorical form that emphatically affirms its opposite: this type of devastating worldly destruction characterizes only the kafur, the intensely and persistently ungrateful. Al-Qurtubi adds that the superlative form 'kafur' carefully distinguishes the Sabaeans' entrenched rejection from ordinary human weakness, showing that divine mercy is patient with failings but not with willful, entrenched ingratitude.

questions.question: Verse 19 records that the Sabaeans asked their Lord to lengthen the distances between their journey-stages. Sayyid Qutb offered a striking spiritual diagnosis of this request in Fi Zilal al-Quran. What did he identify as the true underlying problem?
options: A. They were pursuing military expansion and wanted harder terrain to harden their armies through difficulty
B. They were genuinely curious about distant lands and sought longer stretches of wilderness to explore
C. Their material prosperity had bred spiritual restlessness and boredom — a crisis of meaning masquerading as a material preference, which only gratitude and reconnection with Allah could remedy
D. They feared the proximity of neighboring towns was making trade too easy and cutting into merchants' profits
questions.explanation: Qutb describes this as 'one of the most tragic moments in human history': a people given everything who grew bored with it. He sees it as a profoundly modern problem — the restlessness that material civilization breeds, curable only by gratitude and divine connection, not by more comfort. The verse closes specifying that its lesson is only for the 'sabbar shakur,' the patient and grateful, who alone possess the wisdom to read history with understanding.

questions.question: True or false: Verse 28 declares that the Prophet Muhammad was sent 'comprehensively to all mankind' as a bearer of good news and a warner, explicitly distinguishing his mission from earlier prophets who were each sent to specific peoples or nations.
questions.explanation: Verse 28 uses 'kaffatan lin-nas' (comprehensively to all people) to describe the universal scope of the Prophet's mission. Imam al-Tabari cites the hadith preserved in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim in which the Prophet stated: 'Every prophet was sent to his own nation specifically, but I have been sent to all of humanity.' Ibn Kathir points to the Prophet's letters to foreign rulers as historical confirmation of this universal mandate.

questions.question: Verse 27 commands the Prophet to challenge polytheists: 'Show me those whom you have attached to Him as partners.' According to Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir, what is the significance of closing this verse with the names al-Aziz and al-Hakim rather than simply leaving the challenge unanswered?
options: A. The two names are purely decorative endings that the Quran uses to mark the end of argumentative passages

B. The two names constitute the real answer to the challenge: only Allah combines irresistible power with perfect wisdom, so only He is rationally worthy of exclusive devotion — whereas any alleged partner is both powerless and created
C. The two names indicate that the punishment for shirk will combine physical force and legal judgment in the Hereafter
D. The two names are primarily an address to the angels, instructing them to record the disbelievers' response
questions.explanation: Al-Zuhayli explains that al-Aziz and al-Hakim provide the positive theological answer that demolishes shirk: power without wisdom is tyranny, and wisdom without power is ineffective, but Allah perfectly unites both, making exclusive devotion to Him the only rational foundation for human life. Ibn Uthaymeen extended this point: people may place trust in systems or leaders that have power without wisdom, or wisdom without power — only Allah embodies the perfect union of both.
